title: Local acyclicity extends to locally constant prime-to-characteristic torsion sheaves
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme] which is locally acyclic [def-weil-pbc-local-acyclicity-abelian-sheaf]. Let $G$ be a locally constant abelian sheaf on $X_{\mathrm{et}}$ [def-weil-pbc-abelian-etale-sheaves] [def-constructible-locally-constant]. Suppose that, at every geometric point $\bar x$ of $X$, the group $G_{\bar x}$ [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks] is torsion and every element has finite order prime to the characteristic of the residue field at $\bar x$ (any finite order is allowed in characteristic zero). Then $f$ is locally acyclic relative to $G$ [def-weil-pbc-local-acyclicity-abelian-sheaf]. The stalk groups need not be finite and no single integer annihilating all stalks is required.

proof.text: Fix a geometric point $\bar x$ of $X$, set $\bar s=f\bar x$, and put $T=X_{(\bar x)}$. Choose a member $U\to X$ of a trivialising datum for $G$ and a lift of $\bar x$ to it, and restrict to an affine open containing the lift. The canonical map $T\to U$ in the strict-henselization construction pulls the constant trivialisation on $U$ back to a constant sheaf $\underline N$ on $T$. The pullback-constant isomorphism is natural in $N$. The closed geometric point of $T$ lifts $\bar x$, and the natural germ and inverse-image-stalk isomorphisms identify $\Gamma(T,G|_T)$ with $M=G_{\bar x}$. By the locally constant description of constant sections, $\Gamma(T,\underline N)=N$: any open of a local spectrum containing its closed point is the entire spectrum, so a locally constant map on $T$ is constant. Consequently the chosen trivialisation identifies $G|_T$ with $\underline M$, in such a way that the inverse germ map sends $m\in M$ to its constant section. Pulling back again gives $G|_V\cong\underline M$ on every $V=T\times_{S_{(\bar s)}}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega^{\prime}$.

Let $I$ be the set of subgroups of $M$ generated by finite subsets, ordered by inclusion. It is nonempty and directed: $0$ is a member and the subgroup generated by the union of two finite generating sets contains both subgroups. Every such subgroup $M_i$ is finite. Indeed, if its generators have orders $a_1,\ldots,a_r$, every element has a representative $\sum_j b_jm_j$ with $0\le b_j<a_j$, so there are at most $\prod_j a_j$ elements. Every element of $M_i$ has order prime to the characteristic $p$ at $\bar x$ by the hypothesis on $M$. Every element of $M$ belongs to its singly generated subgroup. For any compatible family of homomorphisms $h_i:M_i\to A$, define $h(m)=h_i(m)$ using a subgroup containing $m$. Directedness and compatibility make this independent of $i$, and a common subgroup containing two elements proves additivity. This is the unique homomorphism extending all $h_i$. Thus the inclusion cocone gives $M=\varinjlim_iM_i$, including the zero group and the case $p=0$.

For each $i$, apply the finitely generated abelian group structure theorem to $M_i$ (its whole finite set is a generating set). Its free summand has rank zero: if the rank were positive, the elements with arbitrary integer in its first coordinate would give infinitely many distinct elements of $M_i$. Hence $M_i\cong\bigoplus_j\mathbf Z/n_{ij}\mathbf Z$, with finitely many $j$ and $n_{ij}$ positive prime powers. Each generator of a cyclic summand maps to an element of $M_i$ of exactly order $n_{ij}$, so $n_{ij}$ is prime to $p$ when $p>0$. Summands with $n_{ij}=1$ are zero and may be retained; the zero group causes no exception.

Fix any geometric point $\bar t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega^{\prime}\to S_{(\bar s)}$ and write $V=T\times_{S_{(\bar s)}}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega^{\prime}$. By local acyclicity of $f$, for each cyclic summand the constant-section map $\mathbf Z/n_{ij}\mathbf Z\to H^0(V,\underline{\mathbf Z/n_{ij}\mathbf Z})$ is an isomorphism, and the groups in degrees $q>0$ vanish. Here the characteristic is that of the residue field at the image of $\bar x$, as in the current definition; its embedding into the geometric field preserves characteristic. Every $n_{ij}$ is positive and prime to this characteristic by step 3 (and all are allowed in characteristic zero). This is exactly the defining condition at $\bar x$; it applies to this $\bar t$ without any algebraicity restriction on its field.

Pass to the finite sums of these coefficients. Constant sheaves preserve finite sums because their functor is left adjoint to global sections. Cohomology preserves these finite sums directly from its resolution formula: choose K-injective resolutions of the summands using [prop-weil-pbc-kinjective-resolutions-exist]. For every acyclic complex $A$, projection to the finitely many summands identifies $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,\bigoplus_j I_j)$ with $\bigoplus_j\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,I_j)$: in each degree the inverse takes finitely many families of maps to their componentwise sum. This commutes with the Hom differential. Kernels and images split componentwise, so this Hom complex is acyclic and the finite sum is K-injective; for the empty sum it is the zero complex. The sum of the resolution maps is a quasi-isomorphism because kernels and images of a finite block-diagonal differential are the sums of the individual kernels and images. Global sections preserve finite products (hence finite sums in abelian groups), and the same kernel/image computation on section complexes gives $H^q(V,\underline{M_i})\cong\bigoplus_jH^q(V,\underline{\mathbf Z/n_{ij}\mathbf Z})$. In degree zero this identification takes a tuple to the sum of its constant sections. Therefore the canonical constant-section map $M_i\to H^0(V,\underline{M_i})$ is an isomorphism and $H^q(V,\underline{M_i})=0$ for $q>0$.

The strict local schemes $T$ and $S_{(\bar s)}$ are spectra of their strict-local rings, so the affine-spectra fibre-product formula identifies $V$ with the spectrum of their tensor product with $\Omega^{\prime}$. Thus $V$ is affine and hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The constant-sheaf functor, being left adjoint, takes the inclusion colimit $M=\varinjlim_iM_i$ to $\underline M=\varinjlim_i\underline{M_i}$. Apply the cohomology filtered-colimit theorem on this qcqs $V$, with the directed set $I$ from step 2. It gives the canonical isomorphism $\varinjlim_iH^q(V,\underline{M_i})\to H^q(V,\underline M)$ for every $q\ge0$. No torsion, finiteness, or Noetherian condition on $V$ is needed by that theorem.

For $q>0$ the colimit in step 6 is a colimit of zero groups, so $H^q(V,\underline M)=0$. For $q=0$ the maps in step 5 form a map of directed systems: for an inclusion $M_i\hookrightarrow M_k$, both composites send $m$ to the constant section with value $m$ in $\underline{M_k}$. Their colimit is therefore the canonical constant-section isomorphism $M\to H^0(V,\underline M)$. By the germ-compatible trivialisation of step 1 this is precisely $\alpha_{G,\bar x,\bar t}$: the inverse germ map sends $m$ to its constant section on $T$, and restriction sends that section to the same constant section on $V$. Thus both clauses of the current definition hold: its specified $\alpha_{G,\bar x,\bar t}$ is invertible, and every positive cohomology group is zero. These conclusions hold for every $\bar t$ and every $\bar x$, which is the definition of local acyclicity relative to $G$.
